addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.2. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

     version stamp so evolutionary change is undetectable, jj
     publishes no compatibility policy, and a `jj --version`
     gate is defeated by users having several jj binaries
     installed.
   - `@`-relative reads ("uncommitted changes right now?")
     need a working-copy snapshot, which is an op-store
     write, so they move with the mutations, not with the
     other reads.
   - Draft ladder, if all three: `-0` open the cycle; `-1`
     settle the version-coupling policy and record it; `-2`
     reads via jj-lib; `-3` mutations + the deferred `@`
     reads; `-4` index-lock retry (bugs.md #1) with a
     `git init --bare` -> gix rider; close-out.
2. **refactor: trapezoid-push + body-intro validation.**
   `vc-x1 trapezoid-push`, a **subcommand** rather than a flag
   on `push` (decided 2026-07-28), publishes a close-out as a
   non-fast-forward merge; body-intro validation rides as
   the first rung. See
   [trapezoid close-out](notes/refactor-20260716.md#stage-trapezoid-close-out)
   and
   [push body-intro validation](notes/refactor-20260716.md#stage-push-body-intro-validation).
   After jj-lib, so the reshape is built in-process.
   - `push` keeps a stateable invariant: it never produces
     a merge. A mode flag that rewires the stage sequence
     would cost that.
   - Shared implementation, not a second copy: the common
     pipeline (preflight, both gates, message, commit-work,
     commit-bot, bookmark-set, push-work, bot squash) moves
     into its own module that both subcommands call, with
     the reshape as the one inserted step. The
     stateless-push cycle shrinks that pipeline first,
     which is what makes the extraction cheap.
   - A backend `trait` (jj today, git or another VCS later)
     is the natural next abstraction if a second backend
     ever appears. Worth converting these concepts to
     traits then, not now: we are committed to jj, and a
     one-implementation trait buys nothing but indirection.
3. **A committed cycle-check runner.** The per-commit flow's
   validation (fmt -> clippy -> test -> install) exists only as
   prose in cycle-protocol.md, so it is recomposed by hand
   every commit, and a hand-composed shell one-liner can
   silently stop checking. Found at the 0.77.0 close-out: in
   `clippy ... 2>&1 | tail -2 && cargo test ...`, the pipeline's
   status is *tail's*, which is always 0, so the `&&` gate
   was decorative and `cargo test` ran even on a run where
   clippy had failed. The failures were caught by reading the
   output, not by any check.

387	## docs: jj-lib design notes + trapezoid recipe
388	
389	Commits: [[8]]
390	
391	A trunk-line interlude between `0.77.0` and the punctuation
392	cycle, carrying two threads from the 2026-07-29 session plus
393	the corrections the `0.77.0` close-out earned by attempting
394	the trapezoid recipe as written.
395	
396	- The op-store coexistence risk was a stub asking for a spike;
397	  it is now answered, and the answer is "unenforceable,
398	  probably fine". Read out of jj-lib 0.41 source against an
399	  installed jj 0.40.0: structural change fails closed, the
400	  index self-heals by reindexing, the op store serializes with
401	  protobuf and carries no version stamp, and jj publishes no
402	  on-disk compatibility policy. We think the residual risk is
403	  low-probability, silent, and low-blast-radius.
404	- The mitigation that looked obvious does not work. A
405	  `jj --version` gate samples what `$PATH` resolves to, which
406	  says nothing about the jj an editor integration or a later
407	  session runs against the same repo. This workspace already
408	  has two.
409	- Consequence for the ladder: taking the coupling is a
410	  decision, not a step 0.78.0 can assume. The index-lock prize
411	  (bugs.md #1) does not require it, since a retry can wrap the
412	  existing spawn today.
413	- The trapezoid recipe's step 4 is `jj git push`, not
414	  `vc-x1 push`. Push runs its whole pipeline or none of it,
415	  and the bot repo is never quiet: by the time the reshape is
416	  done, `.claude` holds the session writes from steps 1-3, so
417	  `commit-bot` wants a title for a work-side publish that
418	  needs nothing but a moved ref.
419	
420	## docs: typeable punctuation
421	
422	Commits:
423	
424	`—`, `–`, `…` and `→` cost nothing to write and are paid on
425	every read: none can be typed at a terminal, so none can be
426	grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as
427	another flag. Nobody chose the 551 sites across the five prose
428	files, they accumulated. AGENTS.md gains the rule that bans
429	them, and the sweep converts what is already written.
430	
431	One commit, no ladder: the rule and the sweep are one idea,
432	and per-file rungs would buy no review value in prose files
433	that have no build and no tests.
434	
435	It started as a question about whether a ladder rung's title
436	and its detail should share a line. They should not, and the
437	em dash was what let them: it joins two things without naming
438	their relationship, which is the failure `### Semicolons
439	inside bullets` already names for `;`. Pulling that thread
440	reached the character itself, and then the whole class. The
441	rule is `### Typeable punctuation only` under
442	[Prose form](/AGENTS.md#prose-form), a sibling to the semicolon
443	rule and cross-linked from its intro. It was designed jointly
444	with the iiac-perf project, whose AGENTS.md carries the same
445	section.
446	
447	### Three roles a banned character can play
448	
449	The rule took four rounds to get right, and each round was the
450	same mistake in a different place: a blanket claim that the
451	next paragraph then contradicted. The settled form sorts by
452	what the character is *doing*, not where it sits.
453	
454	- **Naming it** (`` `…` ``) is a specimen and stays. This is
455	  how the section names the characters it bans.
456	- **Doing a job** (`` `.expect(…)` ``) is a use and converts.
457	  A first draft exempted all code spans, which would have
458	  forbidden the very conversions the sweep had just made.
459	- **Transcribed from outside** (tool output, an error message,
460	  an already-published commit title) keeps its characters,
461	  code span or not. Transcription is not authoring.
462	
463	The third role is why `README.md` still holds four em dashes:
464	its `vc-x1 config` samples transcribe what the installed binary
465	prints, and `src/config_schema.rs` puts em dashes in the `doc:`
466	strings. Converting the samples would make the docs claim
467	output that does not exist. They convert at `0.77.3`, in the
468	same commit that changes the strings.
469	
470	We think the reason this rule needs to be absolute where the
471	semicolon rule is a lean is that the cost is asymmetric: an em
472	dash is free to write and paid on every read, so a soft rule
473	accumulates them. 551 sites in five files is the evidence.
474	
475	### Four banned characters, and an audit that checked three
476	
477	The rule bans four characters: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. Every
478	verification run during the sweep counted three of them. The en
479	dash was never in the audit command, so it was never in the
480	report, so the sweep read as complete while two real sites
481	survived: a section range written `1–8` in TODO.md and a step
482	range written `1–3` in cycle-protocol.md. Both were found by
483	the last check
484	before the commit, which happened to include the fourth
485	character.
486	
487	We think the en dash is the easiest of the four to miss for a
488	reason that will recur: it is the only one with no distinct
489	visual signature at a glance. `…` and `→` are unmistakable, and
490	an em dash is long enough to notice in running prose, but `–`
491	between two numbers looks exactly like the hyphen it should
492	have been. It hides in precisely the construct it is used for.
493	
494	Two consequences worth carrying forward:
495	
496	- **The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it.** A
497	  check that tracks a subset silently reports success. This is
498	  the same defect class as the `clippy ... | tail -2 && cargo
499	  test` gate found at the 0.77.0 close-out, where the pipeline
500	  status came from `tail` and the `&&` was decorative: a
501	  mechanism that looks like a guarantee and is not.
502	- **A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its
503	  character set from one place** shared with the rule's text,
504	  so the two cannot drift. Enumerating the characters a second
505	  time in the checker recreates exactly the gap this cycle hit.
506	
507	The count reported for this cycle, 551 sites, is therefore two
508	low as originally tallied; the corrected total is 553.
509	
510	### An em dash in a heading moves its anchor
511	
512	Found mid-sweep, and it is the one silent failure in the whole
513	change. Stripping the dash leaves the spaces on both sides, so
514	`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while the colon form slugs to
515	`#a-b`. Converting a heading therefore breaks every inbound
516	link to it.
517	
518	Three headings in AGENTS.md and one in refactor-20260716.md
519	were affected; a repo-wide grep found four inbound links, all
520	in the same files. The rule now carries the warning.
521	
522	# References
523

525	[2]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/2424e14f858d "2424e14f858d010e5c07e8821149a114b3d3dda5"

  (bugs.md #1) does not require it, since a retry can wrap the
  existing spawn today.
- The trapezoid recipe's step 4 is `jj git push`, not
  `vc-x1 push`. Push runs its whole pipeline or none of it,
  and the bot repo is never quiet: by the time the reshape is
  done, `.claude` holds the session writes from steps 1-3, so
  `commit-bot` wants a title for a work-side publish that
  needs nothing but a moved ref.

## docs: typeable punctuation

Commits:

`—`, `–`, `…` and `→` cost nothing to write and are paid on
every read: none can be typed at a terminal, so none can be
grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as
another flag. Nobody chose the 551 sites across the five prose
files, they accumulated. AGENTS.md gains the rule that bans
them, and the sweep converts what is already written.

One commit, no ladder: the rule and the sweep are one idea,
and per-file rungs would buy no review value in prose files
that have no build and no tests.

It started as a question about whether a ladder rung's title
and its detail should share a line. They should not, and the
em dash was what let them: it joins two things without naming
their relationship, which is the failure `### Semicolons
inside bullets` already names for `;`. Pulling that thread
reached the character itself, and then the whole class. The
rule is `### Typeable punctuation only` under
[Prose form](/AGENTS.md#prose-form), a sibling to the semicolon
rule and cross-linked from its intro. It was designed jointly
with the iiac-perf project, whose AGENTS.md carries the same
section.

### Three roles a banned character can play

The rule took four rounds to get right, and each round was the
same mistake in a different place: a blanket claim that the
next paragraph then contradicted. The settled form sorts by
what the character is *doing*, not where it sits.

- **Naming it** (`` `…` ``) is a specimen and stays. This is
  how the section names the characters it bans.
- **Doing a job** (`` `.expect(…)` ``) is a use and converts.
  A first draft exempted all code spans, which would have
  forbidden the very conversions the sweep had just made.
- **Transcribed from outside** (tool output, an error message,
  an already-published commit title) keeps its characters,
  code span or not. Transcription is not authoring.

The third role is why `README.md` still holds four em dashes:
its `vc-x1 config` samples transcribe what the installed binary
prints, and `src/config_schema.rs` puts em dashes in the `doc:`
strings. Converting the samples would make the docs claim
output that does not exist. They convert at `0.77.3`, in the
same commit that changes the strings.

We think the reason this rule needs to be absolute where the
semicolon rule is a lean is that the cost is asymmetric: an em
dash is free to write and paid on every read, so a soft rule
accumulates them. 551 sites in five files is the evidence.

### Four banned characters, and an audit that checked three

The rule bans four characters: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. Every
verification run during the sweep counted three of them. The en
dash was never in the audit command, so it was never in the
report, so the sweep read as complete while two real sites
survived: a section range written `1–8` in TODO.md and a step
range written `1–3` in cycle-protocol.md. Both were found by
the last check
before the commit, which happened to include the fourth
character.

We think the en dash is the easiest of the four to miss for a
reason that will recur: it is the only one with no distinct
visual signature at a glance. `…` and `→` are unmistakable, and
an em dash is long enough to notice in running prose, but `–`
between two numbers looks exactly like the hyphen it should
have been. It hides in precisely the construct it is used for.

Two consequences worth carrying forward:

- **The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it.** A
  check that tracks a subset silently reports success. This is
  the same defect class as the `clippy ... | tail -2 && cargo
  test` gate found at the 0.77.0 close-out, where the pipeline
  status came from `tail` and the `&&` was decorative: a
  mechanism that looks like a guarantee and is not.
- **A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its
  character set from one place** shared with the rule's text,
  so the two cannot drift. Enumerating the characters a second
  time in the checker recreates exactly the gap this cycle hit.

The count reported for this cycle, 551 sites, is therefore two
low as originally tallied; the corrected total is 553.

### An em dash in a heading moves its anchor

Found mid-sweep, and it is the one silent failure in the whole
change. Stripping the dash leaves the spaces on both sides, so
`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while the colon form slugs to
`#a-b`. Converting a heading therefore breaks every inbound
link to it.

Three headings in AGENTS.md and one in refactor-20260716.md
were affected; a repo-wide grep found four inbound links, all
in the same files. The rule now carries the warning.

440	
441	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
442	close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
443	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
444	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
445	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
446	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
447	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
448	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
449	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
450	the latter is push's job.
451	
452	#### Details
453	
454	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
455	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
456	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
457	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
458	  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
459	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
460	  once published.
461	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
462	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
463	  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
464	  rung, not the last close-out.
465	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
466	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
467	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
468	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
469	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
470	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
471	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
472	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
473	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
474	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
475	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
476	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
477	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
478	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
479	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
480	  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
481	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
482	  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
483	  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
484	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
485	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
486	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
487	  push force-updates the target.
488	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
489	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
490	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
491	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
492	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
493	
494	#### Recovery
495

file.content:
**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
different operation from committing and publishing, and only
the latter is push's job.

#### Details

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
  once published.
- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
  rung, not the last close-out.
- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
  push force-updates the target.
- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.

#### Recovery

- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.

Dug through the record. Three findings.

## 1. 0.77.4 is not a duplicate of 0.77.2, but the ladder makes it look like one

They're different sweeps with near-identical titles:

- **0.77.2 `docs: typeable punctuation`** (shipped, `62d71818`): the *rule* in AGENTS.md plus the prose sweep. 553 sites across five prose files.
- **0.77.4 `refactor: typeable punctuation in src`**: `src/` only. Real remaining work, and it's a different risk class: `config_schema.rs` `doc:` strings and error/log messages are user-visible output, so the cargo cycle is mandatory, and it unblocks the four README `vc-x1 config` samples that currently transcribe what the binary prints.

Two drifts to fix while we're here:

- `chores-15.md:467` says those README samples "convert at `0.77.3`". Stale: the interlude took 0.77.3, so the src sweep is 0.77.4.
- The ladder entry says "655 em dashes". That is the em-dash count only. Actual `src/` totals: 655 `—`, 166 `→`, 39 `…`, 1 `–` = **861 sites**. That is precisely the defect chores-15 wrote up two sections earlier ("the audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it") reappearing in the plan for the next rung.

## 2. "ochid describe caution" is the 0.77.2 amend incident

I found it in TODO #6 (`squash-push --title` / `--body`), the bullet **"The guard has a hole the flags would close"**: `squash-push` refuses a squash that drops source-only trailers (the 0.65.1 ochid-loss incident), but `jj describe` guards nothing. A user-supplied body silently drops the `ochid:` trailer unless it repeats it. You hit this on 2026-07-29 amending 0.77.2's own close-out bookkeeping: the trailer survived only because it was hand-copied.

So the caution is: **`jj describe` on a commit that carries `ochid:` trailers silently breaks the cross-repo link unless you copy the trailers forward** — and the two-step workaround (`jj describe -r @-` then `squash-push`) is *strictly less safe* than the feature it substitutes for, because it routes around the only check that protects the trailer. `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped ochid by title match, so it's recoverable rather than silent-forever. Nothing in AGENTS.md or cycle-protocol.md says this today; AGENTS.md only says "don't hand-write ochid trailers", which is the opposite direction and reads as reassurance.

## 3. Your reading of "interlude shape" is right, and the facts for it are already scattered

An interlude is an unplanned commit landing between cycles on the trunk line. Everything about it exists, but in four places and never as a definition:

- `TODO.md:46` — `docs:` entries are interludes belonging to no rung.
- `cycle-protocol.md:461` — `<base>` is the parent of the ladder's first rung, *not* the last close-out, because an interlude sits on the trunk line and must stay there. This bit twice (0.76.0, then again at 0.77.0).
- `chores-15.md:375` / TODO #4 — a section with no ladder (a single-commit interlude) keeps its `Commits:` line.
- Numbering by observation only: interludes take a patch bump (0.75.1, 0.76.1, 0.77.1, 0.77.2), never a `-N` rung.

What's missing is the decision rule: **when** does unplanned work become an interlude versus a rung appended to the running cycle, and does an interlude carry a ladder at all.

## The `&&`/`tail` defect is Todo #3, not 0.77.3

`cargo clippy ... 2>&1 | tail -8 && cargo test` takes the pipeline's status from `tail`, which is always 0, so the gate is decorative. That's already captured as Todo #3 ("A committed cycle-check runner") — the fix is a committed runner script, not prose, so it doesn't belong in a docs interlude. chores-15 cites it as the same defect class as the missing en dash in the audit.

## Proposed

Retitle the rung to **`0.77.3 docs: interlude shape + jj describe drops ochid`** (`jj describe` is more greppable than "ochid describe") and scope it to: define the interlude in cycle-protocol.md and pull the four scattered facts under it; add the `jj describe` trailer caution next to the existing "don't hand-write ochid trailers" text in AGENTS.md; fix the chores-15 `0.77.3` -> `0.77.4` reference; and correct the 0.77.4 rung's count to 861 across four characters.

Want me to open 0.77.3 on that scope?

- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:

- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the
installed CLI) while this repo is under active development,
the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle
install never clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name** — the manifest's package name carries a `-dev`
  suffix (`vc-x1` → `vc-x1-dev`); if Rust, `[package].name`,
  so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces
  `<name>-dev` and leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step** — the step already lives in the
  version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V` reports the exact rung);
  a per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and
  litter the install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion** — plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit
  act: a separate clone built at the chosen commit with the
  plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the
  per-commit flow's install.

This project adopted the convention 2026-07-23 (during
0.75.0); projects without external consumers can skip it.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

content.text:
Agreed on both splits. But before you commit to "everywhere in one change," here is what "everywhere" actually is — I counted the whole repo, not just `src/`:

| area | sites |
|---|---|
| `notes/chores/chores-01..15.md` | 1965 |
| `src/` (+ `tests/`) | ~875 |
| other `notes/*.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `support/` | ~805 |
| **total** | **3645** |

The 0.77.2 sweep converted five prose files. `notes/` at large, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and the entire chores archive were never in scope — `versioning.md` alone still has 33, and I hit them while reading it just now.

## Two reasons the chores archive can't ride in a mechanical sweep

**Transcription.** The three-roles rule says text quoted from outside this repo's prose keeps its characters. In `src/` that case is rare. In `chores/` it is everywhere: pasted tool output, quoted error messages, already-published commit titles that must stay byte-identical for `git log --grep`. A sed over 1965 sites would silently corrupt the transcriptions, and it would do so in the one place where the corrupted text is a historical record nobody will re-derive. That is not a sweep, it is 1965 judgment calls.

**Anchors.** Converting a heading moves its slug, and the chores files are the most linked-into surface in the repo — every `[N]:` ref from `TODO.md`, `done.md`, and the refactor notes points at a `chores-NN.md#anchor`. A repo-wide heading conversion breaks inbound links at a scale where the "re-point in the same commit" instruction stops being checkable by eye.

There is also a policy wrinkle: the rule as written says *"It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched."* Sweeping the historical archive isn't executing that rule, it's amending it. Fine to amend — but it should be a stated decision in the same commit, not an implied one.

## What I'd actually do

Split by *risk*, not by directory, and the split falls in a natural place:

- **One change, all live surfaces**: `src/` + `tests/` + all non-chores `notes/*.md` + `ARCHITECTURE.md` + `support/`. ~1680 sites. These are edited and grepped, which is the rule's whole justification. Includes the user-visible strings, so the cargo cycle is mandatory and the four README `vc-x1 config` samples regenerate after `cargo install` in that same commit. Your instinct is right here — this is one idea, and per-file rungs would buy nothing, exactly as chores-15 argued for 0.77.2.
- **The chores archive stays under "converts when touched"**, or becomes its own later rung done with per-hit review. Not the same commit either way.

If you want the archive in too, I'd want it as a separate rung specifically so its diff can be read for transcription damage without 1680 mechanical edits in the way.

## Numbering

Four items now, and one is much bigger than the interludes:

- `0.77.3 docs: interlude shape` — define it, pull the four scattered facts under it
- `0.77.4 docs: jj describe drops ochid` — itself an interlude, demonstrating 0.77.3
- **`0.78.0 refactor: typeable punctuation in source and notes`** — ~1680 sites, mandatory cargo cycle, README regeneration. At that size with a real validation step it reads as a cycle with a ladder, not a patch interlude.

That pushes jj-lib to 0.79.0 and trapezoid-push to 0.80.0. Worth it, I think: calling a 1680-site change with a mandatory cargo cycle a patch bump would be the first interlude that isn't one, in the same breath as we're writing down what an interlude is.

Two open questions for you: does the punctuation sweep earn the minor bump, and does the chores archive convert now, later, or only when touched?

Right, and that's a wording bug in the rule itself, not a nuance on top of it. AGENTS.md says:

> **Banned:** `—`, `–`, `…`, `→` ... Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is absolute

and then, four paragraphs later, says transcribed text keeps its characters. Both can't be true. What is absolute is the **authoring** prohibition; presence in the file is not the thing being forbidden, and can't be, because a transcription that converts is a falsified quote.

So the correct framing is: *we stop typing them; the repo will always contain some.* The three-roles section already got this right — the headline word contradicts its own section.

## The wording fix

Replace "Banned:" with something scoped to the act, e.g. "Never authored: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`", and scope the absoluteness clause: "Unlike the semicolon rule this one is absolute **for text we write**; transcribed text is not ours to change." That makes the specimen/use/transcription split a consequence of the rule rather than an exception carved out of it.

## The consequence that actually matters

chores-15 recorded two forward-looking items that both assume a checkable target:

- "The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it"
- "A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its character set from one place"

A byte scan **cannot** implement this rule. Presence is legitimate, so the target is not zero, and no scanner can tell an authored em dash from a transcribed one — that distinction lives in intent, not in bytes. Any checker written to the current wording will either report thousands of false positives or need an exception list that grows forever.

Two shapes that do work:

- **Baseline delta.** Record per-file counts; the check fails when a count *rises*. Authoring a new one trips it; transcriptions are inert once recorded. No classification needed, and it degrades gracefully — a legitimate new transcription is a one-line baseline update with a reviewer looking at it.
- **Structural exemption.** Require transcriptions to sit in fenced blocks, scan only outside them. Cleaner to check, but it's a new prose constraint and the specimens in AGENTS.md are inline spans, so it needs its own carve-out anyway.

I'd take the baseline delta. It matches what the rule actually is — a ratchet on new authoring — and it makes the sweep's value legible: converting the live surfaces lowers the baseline, and the archive's 1965 sites just sit in it, harmless, until touched.

That also settles your chores-archive question by making it moot: with a delta check, leaving the archive unconverted costs nothing, so "converts when touched" is the right policy and the sweep can stop at the live surfaces.

## Where this lands in the plan

It adds a small amendment to whichever commit does the sweep, and it changes what Todo #3's neighborhood expects from `validate-repo`. Revised:

- `0.77.3 docs: interlude shape`
- `0.77.4 docs: jj describe drops ochid`
- `0.78.0 refactor: typeable punctuation in source and notes` — rule rewording as the first rung (it's the reason the sweep can be bounded), then the ~1680 live-surface sites, README samples regenerated, cargo cycle; chores archive explicitly out of scope with the delta-check rationale recorded.

The rewording is arguably its own docs interlude before the sweep. I'd keep it as the sweep's first rung instead: it's the same idea, and separating them would put a rule change on trunk with nothing yet conforming to it.

content.text:
That instinct is worth taking seriously, and it changes what's worth doing *now* regardless of whether you go through with it.

**What a new repo actually fixes.** The tax you're feeling isn't the em dashes, it's that a convention change costs a corpus sweep — every rule amendment implies touching 15 chores files. That cost scales with history, and vc-x1 has a lot of history. A fresh repo resets it to zero.

**What it doesn't fix.** The conventions accreted because you were learning, not because the repo was old; they'll re-accrete in vc-x2 at the same rate. And the archive is the awkward part: this project's entire thesis is that the "why" is worth preserving alongside the "what." Abandoning 15 chores files is abandoning the thing the dual-repo exists to produce. That's not fatal, but it should be a deliberate act, not a side effect.

**The cheap version of the same win.** The delta-baseline conclusion from a moment ago is, functionally, the restart's main benefit: freeze history, apply conventions going forward, stop paying for the past. You can have that today for one commit.

**Where I think your instinct is straightforwardly right:** it kills most of the 0.78.0 sweep. Split the ~1680 sites by what survives a transition:

- `src/` + `tests/` (~875) carry forward into any successor, whatever it's called. Converting them is never wasted, and the user-visible strings + README samples need doing regardless.
- `notes/*.md` (~805) get curated on the way into a new repo, if there is one. Sweeping them now and curating them later is paying twice.

So the sweep shrinks to source, the rule gets its rewording and a baseline, and notes convert when touched — which is what the rule said in the first place.

**On sequencing.** Finishing the refactor first is right, and for a specific reason: you'd want vc built on the in-process jj-lib facade, not on subprocess spawning you'd then migrate again. 0.78.0 jj-lib and 0.79.0 trapezoid-push are the parts you'd carry over intact. That also means the honest framing of the restart is *graduation*, not rewrite — `vc-x1` was named as experiment 1, and `vc` is what the experiment was for.

One question worth deciding before, not after: does the vc-x1 chores archive go read-only-alongside, get curated down to a distilled "lessons" file, or get left behind entirely? That answer determines how much of the current notes work is worth doing at all, and it's the only part of this that's hard to reverse.

For now I'd do nothing about the restart and just narrow 0.78.0 to source. Want me to open 0.77.3 on interlude shape, or park the ladder and think about vc first?

content.text:
Make it a rider, not a rung.

It's a real hazard for exactly the work you're about to do: `jj describe` is what you reach for during a close-out amend, and both 0.78.0 and 0.79.0 end in close-outs. The 0.77.2 incident happened in precisely that window. So it has operational value now, not archival value.

But it doesn't need its own commit. Four lines in AGENTS.md's `## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)` section, which is where the misleading impression currently forms — that section says "don't hand-write them, `vc-x1 push` injects them," which reads as reassurance that trailers are handled for you. The correction goes right there:

- `jj describe` replaces the entire message; it does not preserve `ochid:`. Amending a commit that has one means copying the trailers forward by hand.
- `squash-push` guards the trailer; `jj describe` guards nothing, so the two-step message fix is less safe than the operation it substitutes for.
- `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped ochid by title match, so it's recoverable.

Then it rides on `0.78.0-0`, the jj-lib cycle's preparation commit, along with the other ladder bookkeeping that's now stale: dropping the 0.77.3/0.77.4 entries from `## In Progress`, and fixing `chores-15.md:467`, which promises the README samples convert at 0.77.3 and now they don't convert at all until someone touches them.

Two things I'd leave alone: TODO #6 keeps its "the guard has a hole" bullet — that's the design record for the eventual fix, and the AGENTS.md note is scaffolding that retires when `squash-push --title`/`--body` lands. And the punctuation rule keeps its current wording; if we're not sweeping, rewording it to "never authored" is a change with no work behind it. Worth doing when the rule next gets touched.

Ready to open 0.78.0 whenever you are — the scope decision from Todo #1 (all three pieces, or defer mutations) is still the thing blocking the ladder.

# Todo Backlog

 Lower-priority `## Todo` entries — the long tail. When an
 entry becomes a priority, move it (and any refs it cites)
 into `TODO.md > ## Todo` at its priority rank (the
 list is strict-ranked, #1 highest), then `fix-todo` to
 renumber.

 Same formatting rules as `TODO.md > ## Todo` — see
 `notes/README.md > ## Todo format`. Run
 `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo-backlog.md` to
 renumber.

## Todo

1. **vc-x1 push: per-repo bookmark names.** Allow code-side
   and `.claude`-side bookmarks to differ; currently
   `.claude` is locked to `main` regardless of the
   app-side `<bookmark>`. Sibling generalization to the
   N:1 / `--squash` / `--merge` work — together they make
   push handle all close-out shapes with arbitrary
   bookmark layouts.
2. **Investigate `linkme` for subcommand registration.**
   Distributed-slice registry — each subcommand registers itself
   at link time; `main.rs` discovers them via the slice rather
   than matching a `Commands` enum. Reduces per-subcommand
   touchpoints from 3 (mod decl + enum variant + match arm) to 1
   (registration). Costs: loses compile-time exhaustiveness
   (missing registration = runtime gap); help-output ordering
   depends on link order unless sorted; macro-magic dependency.

### Amending a message drops the trailer

`jj describe` replaces the whole commit message, so a commit
that already carries an `ochid:` trailer loses it unless the new
body repeats it. This does not contradict "don't hand-write
trailers": push authors a message from scratch and stamps its
own, while an amend edits a message that is already stamped, and
what is already there must be preserved.

- Copy the trailers forward by hand when amending. Hit at the
  0.77.2 amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only
  that way.
- Nothing catches the loss. `squash-push` refuses a squash that
  would drop a trailer, `jj describe` guards nothing, so the
  two-step message fix (`jj describe -r @-`, then
  `squash-push`) is less safe than the one-step operation it
  substitutes for.
- `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped ochid by title match, so
  the loss is recoverable rather than silent-forever.
- Scaffolding until the `squash-push --title` / `--body` Todo
  lands, which closes the hole by keeping the edit on the
  guarded path.

Two separate things. Taking the second first, since it changes what we write.

`jj describe` collides with a documented procedure: the sub-cycle ladder's per-commit contract (`cycle-protocol.md:668`) uses `jj describe` as step 4, on a fresh local scratch commit that has never been published and carries no trailers. A literal "never without coordinating" would put a checkpoint on every rung of every sub-cycle.

The distinction that makes your rule coherent: the hazard is *re*-describing — a commit that is already published, or already stamped with trailers. That's a history rewrite and a silent trailer drop. Naming a never-described local scratch commit is authoring a message for the first time, which has neither property. So I've written it scoped to the rewrite case, with the sub-cycle step called out as the exception. Say the word if you want it absolute instead and I'll widen it and add the coordination checkpoint to the sub-cycle contract.

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
   full suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
descendants auto-rebase.

### Close-out: squash the ladder

When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:

```
jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
```

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.

### Recovery

The principle is the mirror image of the punctuation problem, which is why both came up in the same session. There the word was too strong for a rule with legitimate exceptions, so "banned" made the reader disbelieve a rule they could see being broken all around them. Here the word was too weak for a rule whose exception should be deliberate, so "typically" let a reader stray without noticing they'd chosen anything. Same failure, opposite directions: the wording has to match how much hesitation the deviation deserves. "Will" plus your point that any rule can be broken gets it right, because it makes breaking it an act rather than a default.

Worth writing down as a convention eventually, though I'd leave it for now — we've been trimming convention work, not adding it, and it's captured in this session either way.

  resume: the state file, `--restart` / `--from` / `--status`,

  `.gitignore` coherence check are gone, and so is preflight,

## docs: re-describe rule + defer punctuation sweep

Commits:

Two unrelated threads, both found by reading the `0.77.x`
ladder rather than by doing the work it planned: a `jj describe`
hazard that had been recorded only inside a feature request,
and two planned rungs whose value did not survive scrutiny.

- **Re-describing is coordinate-first.** `jj describe` on a
  published or already-stamped commit is a history rewrite and
  silently drops the `ochid:` trailer, since it replaces the
  whole message and nothing guards it the way `squash-push`
  guards a squash. The hazard is not theoretical: it cost the
  `0.77.2` amend its trailer, which survived only by
  hand-copying. AGENTS.md carries the rule, next to the ochid
  semantics rather than inside the Todo that will eventually
  fix it.
- **The sub-cycle ladder is the named exception**, and it
  needed saying from both ends. Ladder commits never leave the
  machine, so they carry no trailer and step 4's `describe` is
  first-time authoring, not a rewrite. cycle-protocol says so
  at the per-Work-commit contract and again at the Close-out
  squash, which is the ladder's single push and where the
  trailer is stamped.
- **`typically` became `will`** in the sub-cycle intro, since
  the local-only claim is flat and a hedge in the same section
  undercut it.
- **Two rungs left the ladder**: the `src` punctuation sweep to
  `## Todo`, interlude shape to the backlog.

### Wording strength should match the deviation it invites

The session hit the same calibration error twice, pointing
opposite ways, which is what made it visible.

- `Banned:` in the punctuation rule was too strong for a rule
  with legitimate exceptions, so the section spent four
  paragraphs contradicting its own first word.
- `typically` in the sub-cycle intro was too weak for a rule
  whose exception should be deliberate, letting a reader stray
  without noticing a choice had been made.

We think the useful test is not "is this rule absolute" but
"how much hesitation should breaking it cost". Any rule here
can be broken; the wording decides whether breaking it is an
act or a default.

### Why the source sweep left the ladder

The rule cannot be enforced at the byte level, and noticing
that changed the sweep's shape and its checker both.

- **`Banned` is not what the rule means.** Transcribed tool
  output and published commit titles keep their characters,
  so presence in a file is legitimate and the prohibition is
  on *authoring*. The rewording is now the first step of the
  `## Todo` entry, because it is what bounds the sweep.
- **Scope shrank to what carries forward.** `src/` and
  `tests/` (~875 sites, four characters, not the 655 em dashes
  the retired rung counted) convert; `notes/` (~805) and the
  chores archive (1965) stay under "converts when touched".
  The archive is thick with transcription that must not
  convert, and heading conversions move anchors the notes
  files link into.
- **A `validate-repo` byte scan cannot implement this**, since
  no scanner separates authored from transcribed. The backlog
  entry now asks for a per-file count baseline that fails on a
  rise, which supersedes the note two sections above asking
  the checker to read its character set from one place.

  needed saying from both ends. Ladder commits never leave the
  machine, so they carry no trailer and step 4's `describe` is
  first-time authoring, not a rewrite. cycle-protocol says so
  at the per-Work-commit contract and again at the Close-out
  squash, which is the ladder's single push and where the
  trailer is stamped.

  the local-only claim is flat and a hedge in the same section
  undercut it.

  `## Todo`, interlude shape to the backlog.

### Wording strength should match the deviation it invites

The session hit the same calibration error twice, pointing
opposite ways, which is what made it visible.

- `Banned:` in the punctuation rule was too strong for a rule
  with legitimate exceptions, so the section spent four
  paragraphs contradicting its own first word.
- `typically` in the sub-cycle intro was too weak for a rule
  whose exception should be deliberate, letting a reader stray
  without noticing a choice had been made.

We think the useful test is not "is this rule absolute" but
"how much hesitation should breaking it cost". Any rule here
can be broken; the wording decides whether breaking it is an
act or a default.

### Why the source sweep left the ladder

The rule cannot be enforced at the byte level, and noticing
that changed the sweep's shape and its checker both.

- **`Banned` is not what the rule means.** Transcribed tool
  output and published commit titles keep their characters,
  so presence in a file is legitimate and the prohibition is
  on *authoring*. The rewording is now the first step of the
  `## Todo` entry, because it is what bounds the sweep.
- **Scope shrank to what carries forward.** `src/` and
  `tests/` (~875 sites, four characters, not the 655 em dashes
  the retired rung counted) convert; `notes/` (~805) and the
  chores archive (1965) stay under "converts when touched".
  The archive is thick with transcription that must not
  convert, and heading conversions move anchors the notes
  files link into.
- **A `validate-repo` byte scan cannot implement this**, since
  no scanner separates authored from transcribed. The backlog
  entry now asks for a per-file count baseline that fails on a
  rise, which supersedes the note two sections above asking
  the checker to read its character set from one place.

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>

content.text:
Agreed on the first half, with a caveat on the second.

**"No mechanism exists" looks right.** Push has a single message stage — the help text lists it as one stage feeding both `commit-work` and `commit-bot`, and `--title`/`--body` are singular. So `:294` isn't describing behavior, it's describing an intention nobody built. That's worse than saying nothing: it reads as a rule being violated, which is exactly how I reported it a minute ago. A protocol that documents a capability the tool lacks manufactures false defects.

**"Nothing different to say" I'd put differently.** There *is* distinct content — this session covered the vc-x2 question, the scope debate, two rounds of wording calibration, none of which appear in the work diff. So it isn't that the session has nothing to say. It's that everything it would say is already recorded better twice over: the transcript is the verbatim record, and the chores section is the curated one. A hand-written bot body would be a third, worse copy that drifts from both. Same reasoning that keeps the edit list out of chores, pointed the other way.

**The real defect isn't duplication, it's misdescription.** The bot commit's diff is one file, the session `.jsonl`. Its body currently claims changes to `AGENTS.md`, `Cargo.toml`, `notes/cycle-protocol.md` and four others — none of which are in that diff. Someone reading `git log` in the bot repo alone is told the commit did things it didn't do. Identical bodies are fine when the body is a summary; they're wrong when the body is a file list, which is what the work-repo convention mandates.

So if that line gets rewritten, I don't think the target is "different bodies." It's deciding what a bot commit's body is *for* given that the link and the transcript already carry the value. Title plus `ochid:` alone would be defensible, or the shared title with a single line naming the session rather than the files. Both are honest about a one-file diff in a way the current output isn't.

Worth noting this is the second line this session that stated an aspiration as a mechanism — `Banned:` was the other. Both survived a long time because nothing checks prose against behavior.

content.text:
You're right, and it's wrong in both directions. This session has produced one commit so far and will produce more; each of those commits contains an *append-slice* of the same transcript file, not a session. And nothing stops the opposite: if you'd run two `claude` invocations before pushing, one commit would carry two transcript files.

The boundary a bot commit actually respects is the **push**, not the session. That's the fix — the sentence claims a unit the data model doesn't implement.

On what a session is: I'd argue the data already committed to an answer, and it's your first one. The transcript is one file per `claude` invocation, named for its session id, so process-lifetime is the only definition with a concrete artifact behind it. The ladder notion is a work-repo concept — a unit of *work*, which can span sessions or sit several to a session — and conflating them is what produced the false sentence. Worth keeping those words apart.

Which suggests dodging the word entirely, since the README doesn't need to define it:

```
Each commit here records the transcript written since the
previous commit, usually a slice of a conversation still in
progress, and is paired with a commit in the work repo,
cross-referenced by an `ochid:` trailer in both directions.
Its diff is one or more transcript files, but its body is the
**work** commit's body: a file-by-file list of what changed
over there.
```

That's true regardless of which definition you land on, and "slice of a conversation still in progress" is the part a reader most needs, since it explains why consecutive commits touch the same file.

Your zero-commit case is a real wrinkle and the framing above survives it, though barely: that conversation's transcript isn't lost, it lands in whatever commit comes next, so a bot commit can carry a conversation that produced nothing alongside a body describing work-repo changes from a different one. Rare, and I wouldn't write it into the README.

The pure-conversation repo you floated is a different shape entirely — a bot repo with no partner, where the `ochid:` half of the convention has nothing to point at and the commit body would have to describe the conversation itself. That's the one case where the body genuinely can't be borrowed. Interesting, and I'd leave it out of this edit.

Want me to swap that sentence in?

You're right, I overreached. I checked, and the data doesn't support "one file per invocation."

What is verified: one `sessionId` per file — the current transcript contains exactly one, so the file is keyed to a *session id*, not to a process. And session ids outlive processes. Nine files in `.claude` contain internal gaps over six hours, the largest 23.6h, with two others at 19.6h and 17.6h:

```
86fb7a89-...jsonl   23.6h gap
c5d1ebdc-...jsonl   19.6h gap
d0d49552-...jsonl   17.6h gap
```

A single file spanning a day-long gap is one conversation continued across separate sittings. We think that's `--resume` / `--continue` reattaching to an existing id, though a terminal left open overnight would look identical from the timestamps alone, and I can't distinguish those from the transcript.

The other direction almost certainly breaks too: we think `/clear` mints a new session id without restarting the process, which would put two files under one invocation. Several same-day file pairs are consistent with that — `00690083` and `663b876c` are two minutes apart on May 30 — but consistent isn't evidence, since a quick exit and restart looks the same.

So the honest invariant is just: **one file per session id**, and session id maps to neither invocation nor sitting reliably in either direction. Which makes it a poor thing to define "session" by after all — it's stable as an identifier and unstable as a unit of anything.

The good news is the proposed README text doesn't depend on any of this. It says the commit records the transcript written since the previous commit, usually a slice of a conversation still in progress. That's true whether a conversation spans one sitting or five, and whether `/clear` split it. It was my justification in conversation that was wrong, not the wording — and it's an argument for keeping the word "session" out of the README, now more strongly than before.

Still want that sentence swapped in?

# vc-x1-bot-repo-template

This is the bot repo of a dual-repo convention for using
a bot to help in the development of a coding project. The goal
is that this bot repo contains the "why" and "how", while the
partner main repo contains the "what". The key to the convention
is each change is cross-referenced to the other. Thus there
is a coherent story of the development of the project across time.

## Reading a commit here

Each commit in this repo records one session and is paired with
a commit in the work repo, cross-referenced by an `ochid:`
trailer in both directions. Its diff is a single session
transcript file, but its body is the **work** commit's body: a
file-by-file list of what changed over there.

- That is deliberate. The pair's story reads whole from either
  side, so `git log` here says what a session accomplished

content.text:
**Location:** `../vc-x1-bot-repo-template/README.md`, lines 12-16 — the intro paragraph of the `## Reading a commit here` section I added. The two bullets below it (18-23) stay, except line 19 also says "session" and would need the same treatment.

**Currently:**
```
Each commit in this repo records one session and is paired with
a commit in the work repo, cross-referenced by an `ochid:`
trailer in both directions. Its diff is a single session
transcript file, but its body is the **work** commit's body: a
file-by-file list of what changed over there.
```

**Proposed:**
```
Each commit here records the transcript written since the
previous commit, usually a slice of a conversation still in
progress, and is paired with a commit in the work repo,
cross-referenced by an `ochid:` trailer in both directions.
Its diff is one or more transcript files, but its body is the
**work** commit's body: a file-by-file list of what changed
over there.
```

Three changes: "records one session" becomes "records the transcript written since the previous commit," which is the push boundary rather than a session boundary; "usually a slice of a conversation still in progress" explains why consecutive commits keep touching the same file; and "a single session transcript file" becomes "one or more transcript files," since nothing stops two conversations landing in one push.

And line 19, which I'd change in the same edit since it carries the same false unit:

```
- That is deliberate. The pair's story reads whole from either
  side, so `git log` here says what the work was without
  switching repos.
```

That drops "what a session accomplished." The word "session" then appears nowhere in the section, which is the point — the README doesn't need a definition we can't make stick.

## Stage: jj-lib migration

Migrate the facade internals to jj-lib (already a dependency
for read-only commands); removes jj and git spawning
entirely.

- Reads first: `jj log` templates become `Commit` accessors
  (the `src/jj.rs` facade internals; `common::load_repo` /
  `resolve_revset` are the existing in-process machinery).
  Caveat: queries against `@` rely on the spawned CLI's
  working-copy auto-snapshot, since push asks "uncommitted
  changes *right now*?", so the in-process form must
  snapshot first, and a snapshot is an op-store write:
  those reads move with the mutation lift, not before.
- Then mutations: commit, describe, bookmark set/track,
  fetch, push, which is the workspace/transaction/op-store
  lift.
- The index-lock retry loop becomes ours (catch, back off,
  retry) with real error types, the fix vehicle for the
  bugs.md `bookmark-set` lock race [[1]].
- `LocalBareInit`'s `git init --bare` becomes a gix call
  (jj-lib already pulls gix in).

## Stage: push body-intro validation

content.content:
564	## Access rule
565	
566	Today's implicit rule (read-only display commands use jj-lib
567	in-process, mutating commands shell out) dissolves once
568	mutations are in-process; ARCHITECTURE.md states the end state
569	instead.
570	
571	## Out of scope: still spawned
572	
573	- `gh` (remote provisioning) and `$EDITOR` stay spawned by
574	  design.
575	- The `vc-x1 sync --check` self-spawn goes away when the
576	  Todo "sync follow-up: push preflight in-process" lands:
577	  same direction, independently shippable, not part of this
578	  program.
579	- Beneficiary: the Todo "Run validate-bot at every vc-x1
580	  invocation", whose per-invocation jj spawn becomes an
581	  in-process read.
582	
583	## Design risk: op-store coexistence
584	
585	In-process op-store writes must coexist with the user's
586	external `jj` CLI driving the same repos. Investigated
587	2026-07-29 (jj-lib 0.41 source, installed jj 0.40.0, jj's
588	published docs). Findings, and why the obvious mitigation
589	does not work:
590	
591	- **Today there is no risk at all.** vc-x1 spawns the user's
592	  `jj` for every mutation, so it inherits their version. The
593	  migration *introduces* the coupling; it does not inherit
594	  one.
595	- **Structural change fails closed.** `repo.rs:491-569` /
596	  `workspace.rs:513` raise `StoreLoadError::UnsupportedType`
597	  when a `type` file names a backend the library lacks, so a
598	  future `op_store/type` we don't know is a hard error, not a
599	  guess.
600	- **The index self-heals.** It carries an explicit format
601	  version (`COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6`,
602	  checked at `default_index/readonly.rs:303`), and
603	  `default_index/store.rs:560` responds to a mismatch by
604	  reindexing, not erroring. Derived data; costs time only.
605	  Reading those bytes ourselves is inert (it does not
606	  trigger the rebuild), but the constant is `pub(super)`, so
607	  a check of our own would duplicate a private constant and
608	  an internal file layout.
609	- **The op store has no version stamp.** It serializes with
610	  protobuf (`simple_op_store.rs:159-218`), whose evolution
611	  rule is that unknown fields are skipped. So an evolutionary
612	  change (same backend type, new fields) is *undetectable*
613	  by construction: a reader cannot distinguish "field absent"
614	  from "field present and unknown to me". The realistic
615	  failure is silent information loss, not corruption.
616	- **jj publishes no compatibility policy.** Checked the core
617	  tenets, architecture, and concurrency pages: no stability
618	  guarantee for on-disk formats, and only a bare footnote
619	  mentioning "automatic upgrades of the repo format" with no
620	  detail. Everything above is behavior read out of one
621	  version's source, which they are free to change.
622	- **Concurrent writers are by design**, which helps the other
623	  half of the question: "To avoid depending on lock files,
624	  Jujutsu takes a different approach by accepting that
625	  concurrent changes can always happen" (concurrency page).
626	  Operations are content-addressed and op heads are tracked
627	  by filename.
628	- **A `jj --version` check does not work.** Users can have
629	  several jj binaries installed (this workspace has both
630	  `vc-x1` and `vc-x1-dev`); what our `$PATH` resolves to says
631	  nothing about what an editor integration, another shell, or
632	  a later session will run against the same repo. The check
