## Access rule

Today's implicit rule (read-only display commands use jj-lib
in-process, mutating commands shell out) dissolves once
mutations are in-process; ARCHITECTURE.md states the end state
instead.

## Out of scope: still spawned

- `gh` (remote provisioning) and `$EDITOR` stay spawned by
  design.
- The `vc-x1 sync --check` self-spawn goes away when the
  Todo "sync follow-up: push preflight in-process" lands:
  same direction, independently shippable, not part of this
  program.
- Beneficiary: the Todo "Run validate-bot at every vc-x1
  invocation", whose per-invocation jj spawn becomes an
  in-process read.

## Design risk: op-store coexistence

In-process op-store writes must coexist with the user's
external `jj` CLI driving the same repos. Investigated
2026-07-29 (jj-lib 0.41 source, installed jj 0.40.0, jj's
published docs). Findings, and why the obvious mitigation
does not work:

- **Today there is no risk at all.** vc-x1 spawns the user's
  `jj` for every mutation, so it inherits their version. The
  migration *introduces* the coupling; it does not inherit
  one.
- **Structural change fails closed.** `repo.rs:491-569` /
  `workspace.rs:513` raise `StoreLoadError::UnsupportedType`
  when a `type` file names a backend the library lacks, so a
  future `op_store/type` we don't know is a hard error, not a
  guess.
- **The index self-heals.** It carries an explicit format
  version (`COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6`,
  checked at `default_index/readonly.rs:303`), and
  `default_index/store.rs:560` responds to a mismatch by
  reindexing, not erroring. Derived data; costs time only.
  Reading those bytes ourselves is inert (it does not
  trigger the rebuild), but the constant is `pub(super)`, so
  a check of our own would duplicate a private constant and
  an internal file layout.
- **The op store has no version stamp.** It serializes with
  protobuf (`simple_op_store.rs:159-218`), whose evolution
  rule is that unknown fields are skipped. So an evolutionary
  change (same backend type, new fields) is *undetectable*
  by construction: a reader cannot distinguish "field absent"
  from "field present and unknown to me". The realistic
  failure is silent information loss, not corruption.
- **jj publishes no compatibility policy.** Checked the core
  tenets, architecture, and concurrency pages: no stability
  guarantee for on-disk formats, and only a bare footnote
  mentioning "automatic upgrades of the repo format" with no
  detail. Everything above is behavior read out of one
  version's source, which they are free to change.
- **Concurrent writers are by design**, which helps the other
  half of the question: "To avoid depending on lock files,
  Jujutsu takes a different approach by accepting that
  concurrent changes can always happen" (concurrency page).
  Operations are content-addressed and op heads are tracked
  by filename.
- **A `jj --version` check does not work.** Users can have
  several jj binaries installed (this workspace has both
  `vc-x1` and `vc-x1-dev`); what our `$PATH` resolves to says
  nothing about what an editor integration, another shell, or
  a later session will run against the same repo. The check
  is a sample, not a gate.

We think the residual risk is therefore low-probability,
silent, and low-blast-radius, but it cannot be enforced
away, so taking it on should be a decision rather than a
step the ladder assumes.

content.text:
## What the mutation lift actually is

Today every mutation is a subprocess. `stage_bookmark_set` (`src/push.rs:638`) is two `run("jj", ...)` calls, and the log line it prints is literally the command:

```rust
run("jj", &["bookmark", "set", bk, "-r", "@-", "-R", &work_arg], root)?;
run("jj", &["bookmark", "set", BOT_BOOKMARK, "-r", "@-", "-R", &bot_arg], root)?;
```

In-process, that becomes: open the `Workspace`, load the `Repo`, `start_transaction()`, mutate the view's bookmark target, commit the transaction. That last step writes a new operation into `.jj/repo/op_store` and moves the op head. That write is the whole risk surface — reads never touch it, which is why the program splits reads from mutations.

The full set is small: commit, describe, bookmark set/track, git fetch, git push.

One clarification, since it confused me a minute ago: the `(in-process)` in push's `squash-push-bot` log line means the *stage* no longer self-spawns `vc-x1 squash-push` as a subprocess. `squash_push.rs:276-310` still shells out to `jj` for the squash, the bookmark set, and the push. So the coexistence risk genuinely has not been taken yet — the notes are right that the migration introduces it rather than inheriting it.

## The concrete example, end to end

Bugs.md #1: `bookmark-set` fails with

```
Failed to reset Git HEAD state ... could not acquire lock for
`.git/index` ... after 1 attempt(s)
```

Four occurrences, always that stage, always transient — we think a git-aware watcher (shell prompt, editor) grabs the index while jj is resetting git HEAD, and jj gives up after one attempt.

- **Spawned + retry:** wrap the `run` call, match the stderr string, sleep, retry. Roughly five lines. Fragile in the specific way the program exists to kill: that string is jj's UI text, and it changes when jj rewords an error.
- **jj-lib + retry:** the same failure arrives as a typed error from the git backend, matched on variant, retried in a loop we own.

The important part: **jj-lib does not fix the bug.** The lock contention is external, and a colocated repo still exports refs to `.git` in-process, so the race is identical. What changes is the quality of the error handling around it. The prize is not the retry, it's not string-matching.

## Why spawning might be better

- **Coexistence, the one that can't be undone.** Spawning means vc-x1 can never write an operation the user's `jj` can't read, because their `jj` *is* the writer. Link jj-lib and vc-x1 becomes a second, independent writer against the same op store, which has no version stamp, no published compatibility policy, and no workable gate (a `jj --version` check samples `$PATH`, which says nothing about what an editor integration runs an hour later). The failure mode is silent information loss.
- **The log is a reproduction script.** Every mutation currently prints the exact command you can paste into a terminal. That's not incidental — it's how the 0.77.0 close-out debugging worked, and how a user recovers from a half-finished push. A transaction can be logged but not pasted.
- **The CLI is a more stable contract than the library.** `jj bookmark set` has defined semantics jj tests and documents. Reimplementing it as a transaction means reimplementing those semantics, including what it does about remote tracking and working-copy state. A subtle divergence is a bug class that does not exist while we spawn.
- **Snapshot semantics become ours.** The notes already flag this: the spawned CLI auto-snapshots, which is why "uncommitted changes right now?" works. In-process we choose when to snapshot, and choosing wrong changes the answer.
- **Upgrades are free today.** jj-lib is 0.41 with no stability promise. Spawning tracks the user's jj upgrades at zero cost; linking puts us on a bump treadmill where a version change can alter on-disk behavior, not just compilation.

The case for jj-lib is real too — typed errors, no `$PATH` dependency, no stderr parsing, no process cost, and it is the program's stated goal. But those are quality-of-implementation wins, and the coexistence cost is a permanent structural one.

## My view

Reads are close to free and clearly worth doing. Mutations I'd want a reason for beyond "the program said so," and the reason usually offered — the index-lock fix — turns out not to require them. The strongest argument *for* going ahead anyway is that stopping halfway leaves two mechanisms in the codebase permanently, which is its own tax and the thing the DRY-facade stage was fighting.

**The plain version:** right now vc-x1 gets its work done by running the same `jj` commands you'd type yourself, so it can never disagree with your copy of jj and you can always see and rerun exactly what it did. Building jj's engine into vc-x1 instead makes its errors much easier to handle properly, but it also makes vc-x1 a second program writing to the same files your jj writes to, with no way to check the two still agree. The bug everyone wants fixed can be fixed either way, so the real question is whether cleaner error handling is worth giving that up.

content.text:
Your framing changes my read of this, and I think it also shows the notes' dismissal is overstated.

**Why the gate is better-targeted than "a `jj --version` check does not work" allows.** That bullet evaluates the check as a compatibility oracle, which it isn't. As a *write guard* it lines up with the actual risk direction:

- The dangerous direction is an old jj reading an op we wrote with a newer jj-lib — protobuf skips unknown fields, so it's silent loss.
- The safe direction, their newer jj reading our older op, is something jj must support anyway, since their own older jj wrote ops into that repo before we ever ran.
- So our only real obligation is: never write an op newer than the oldest jj they'll run. Equality at write time enforces exactly that, and it's conservative — identical versions means identical code, not a guess about format evolution.

The multi-binary objection also weakens under that framing. If a second jj binary writes ops the first can't read, that's jj-versus-jj, which is jj's problem and exists with or without us.

**It would refuse to run today.** Installed `jj 0.40.0`, and `Cargo.lock` resolves `jj-lib 0.41.0`. So the gate isn't hypothetical friction — it fires on the current workspace, which is a useful thing to know before building it.

**The cost is an operational coupling, and it lands in a bad place.** Every jj release would block the user from running vc-x1 until we ship a matching build. That's a hard stop in the middle of the commit workflow, caused by an upgrade that is usually harmless. Silent-and-rare becomes loud-and-frequent. Worth it only if the loudness is tunable, which I think it is:

- **Gate the write path, not startup.** Reads never touch the op store, so they should work at any version. Only the mutation stages refuse. Cuts the blast radius to the operation that actually carries the risk.
- **Refuse by default, with an explicit override.** A `--allow-jj-version-mismatch` flag (or a config key) keeps the user unblocked when they've decided the risk is acceptable, and makes taking it a deliberate act rather than a default — the same calibration as `typically` versus `will`.
- **Prefer the `.vc-config.toml` pin over `$PATH` or an env var.** The pin is a *declaration* of which jj this repo is for; the other two are samples of what one shell happens to resolve. Same reason the notes rejected the naive check.

One implementation wrinkle worth naming early: we'd need jj-lib's version at runtime, which means capturing it at build time from Cargo metadata rather than hardcoding a constant that drifts from the dependency. And the comparison itself requires spawning `jj --version` — a spawn the program keeps forever, in the migration whose purpose is ending spawning. Not a problem, but it should be a deliberate exception rather than an embarrassment discovered later.

**Where this leaves the scope decision.** With a write-path gate plus a config pin, the coexistence objection moves from "unenforceable, accept it" to "enforceable at a known operational cost", which is a much easier thing to say yes to. That makes taking mutations in 0.78.0 more defensible than it looked yesterday, and it means the risk section's last two bullets need revising when the cycle opens — they currently record a conclusion this supersedes.

**The plain version:** the worry is that vc-x1 could write something into the repo that your installed jj is too old to understand, and lose information quietly. Checking at startup that the two match does prevent that, because if they're the same version they're the same code. The catch is that you'd be locked out of vc-x1 every time you upgrade jj until a matching vc-x1 exists. That's tolerable if the check only blocks the operations that actually write, lets you override it deliberately, and reads which jj to expect from the repo's own config rather than guessing from your shell.

Right, and it's actually a three-way spread: installed `jj 0.40.0`, our pin `jj-lib 0.41`, and `jj-cli` is now published at **0.43.0**. Nobody noticed any of that drift, which is the argument for your gate in miniature.

The reassuring part: today the mismatch is completely inert. Every mutation spawns your `jj`, so jj-lib 0.41 never writes an operation — it only reads. The version skew starts mattering at exactly the moment mutations move in-process, and not a day earlier. Which means aligning the versions isn't a separate chore; it's a precondition of that rung, and the rung can't honestly claim to be done without it.

One wrinkle for whenever the check gets built: your jj is a git build, `0.40.0-941d0290f5511db1d1cf8e4fe7365ba7d1828ea0`, not the released 0.40.0. So strict equality has to decide what it's comparing. The semver triple is the only thing both sides can produce, and it doesn't identify a git build at an arbitrary commit — two binaries can both say `0.40.0` and be different code. Comparing triples is still worth doing, but it's a weaker guarantee than "identical versions means identical code," and the note should say so rather than overclaim.

When the rung comes, the cleanest alignment is probably installing a released `jj-cli` and pinning `jj-lib` to the same triple, so both sides come from crates.io and equality means what it says. Nothing to do now.

That leaves our side as the odd one out — `Cargo.toml` still pins `jj-lib = "0.41"`, so the gap is now two releases in the other direction. Aligning it to `0.43` is the obvious move, but it isn't necessarily a one-line change: jj-lib is pre-1.0 and 0.41 -> 0.43 spans two releases of a library with no stability promise, so the read-side calls we already use (`load_repo`, `resolve_revset`, the `Commit` accessors) may have shifted. That's exactly the treadmill cost I listed as an argument for spawning, arriving on schedule.

It also wants to be a commit rather than a drive-by, since it touches `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` and needs the full cargo cycle — reads go through jj-lib today, so a break there is a real break.

Want me to probe it? Bump the pin, run `cargo check`, and report how much drift there is, reverting either way. That number is useful input to the 0.78.0 ladder: if it's clean, the alignment is a cheap first rung; if it isn't, the mutations decision gets a concrete price tag attached to it.

content.text:
Fixed, and the cargo cycle is green: fmt applied, clippy clean on `--all-targets`, and 510 tests pass across all 7 binaries with 0 failures. `cargo install` not run yet.

**The three changes:**

- `src/common.rs:504` — dropped `use_glob_by_default: false`. The field is gone in 0.43, not renamed.
- `src/common.rs:518` — `commit_change_ids()` now returns `LocalBoxStream`, so the `for` loop became `while let Some(result) = stream.next().block_on()`. `pollster::FutureExt` was already imported for `load_at_head()`, so the shape matches what the file already did.
- `Cargo.toml` — added `futures = "0.3"`. The judgment call: the `Revset` trait offers no blocking iterator any more (`stream`, `commit_change_ids`, `stream_graph` all return `LocalBoxStream`), so consuming one needs `StreamExt`. `futures 0.3.33` was already in `Cargo.lock` via jj-lib, so this promotes a transitive dep to a direct one rather than adding weight. The alternative was hand-rolling a poll loop with a no-op waker, which is worse code for no gain.

**One thing the compiler did not tell you.** `use_glob_by_default` wasn't merely deleted — the behavior it selected changed. In 0.41:

```rust
let default_kind = if context.use_glob_by_default { "glob" } else { "substring" };
```

In 0.43, `expect_string_expression` builds `StringPattern::glob(value)` unconditionally. We were passing `false`, so we were on **substring** matching, and 0.43 moved us to **glob** with no opt-out. A revset like `description(foo)` used to match any description containing "foo" and now matches only the literal "foo".

Nothing of ours breaks: our revsets are `all()`, `children(<hex>)`, and bare change ids, none of which take string patterns. But a user-supplied `-r 'description(foo)'` now means something different than it did this morning.

That's worth noting because of where we just were in the conversation. The API break was loud and took ten minutes; the semantic change rode in silently under it, and `cargo check` passing is precisely the signal that would have told us we were done. Two releases of a pre-1.0 library, and one of each kind. It's a small argument for the version gate and a larger one for not treating a green build as evidence that a jj-lib bump was behavior-preserving.

The working copy now has real code changes on top of a clean repo, so they need a commit home — natural as `0.78.0-0`, or as a standalone `build:` commit if you'd rather the alignment land before the cycle opens.

content.text:
I'm not sure which "for" you're pointing at — I wrote "if you'd rather the alignment land before the cycle opens," so I think we're already agreeing on position. Say more if I'm missing a distinction.

On the substance: the one thing that can't vary is atomicity. The bump and the two API fixes have to be the same commit — `Cargo.toml` at 0.43 without the fixes doesn't compile, and the fixes without the bump don't compile against 0.41. So there's no "before the jj-lib bump" commit to make; there's one commit's worth of work, and only its *position* is open.

Standalone and before the cycle is the right call, for three reasons:

- It isn't migration work. It's keeping the existing read-side compiling against the jj you now have installed, which is true whichever way the mutations decision goes.
- It leaves 0.78.0 starting from a repo already aligned with jj 0.43, so the cycle's diffs are migration-only rather than migration-plus-repair. That matters for bisection, which is the ladder's stated purpose.
- If the scope decision lands on "retry only, no jj-lib yet," this commit is still needed and still correct. Folding it into a cycle that might not happen would be the wrong bet.

That makes it `0.77.4`, a trunk-line interlude, and worth noting for the third time today: 0.78.0's trapezoid `<base>` becomes this commit, not `0.77.3`.

`build:` is the right type — Conventional Commits scopes it to build system and dependency changes, which is exactly this.

The one open question is whether the glob-semantics change deserves anything beyond the commit body. It's a behavior change we inherited rather than made, it doesn't affect our own revsets, and it would affect a user typing `-r 'description(foo)'`. I'd put it in the commit body and add a line to `notes/bugs.md` or the refactor notes only if you think a user-facing revset behavior change should be discoverable later. My inclination is the commit body is enough.

The compiler reported the removed field. It could not report
that the behavior the field selected had also changed, and
that is the more interesting half.

- In 0.41 the default string-pattern kind was chosen by the

  which take string patterns. A user-supplied
  `-r 'description(foo)'` does change.

We think this is worth recording because of what it says
about the mutation decision this cycle is deciding. Two
releases of a pre-1.0 library produced one break the compiler
caught and one it structurally could not, and the green build
that followed the fix was not evidence the bump preserved
behavior. That asymmetry is the treadmill cost, and it is

on the trunk line before the cycle rather than inside it.

- `RevsetParseContext::use_glob_by_default` is gone in 0.43,
  so the field assignment goes with it.
- `Revset::commit_change_ids()` returns a `LocalBoxStream`
  rather than an iterator. Consumed with `StreamExt::next`
  driven by the `pollster` `block_on` the file already used
  for `load_at_head()`.
- `futures` is promoted from a transitive dependency to a
  direct one. The `Revset` trait offers no blocking iterator
  any more, so consuming any of its three methods needs
  `StreamExt`; the alternative was a hand-rolled poll loop
  with a no-op waker.

### A silent semantic change under a loud API break

The compiler reported the removed field. It could not report
that the behavior the field selected had also changed, and
that is the more interesting half.

- In 0.41 the default string-pattern kind was chosen by the
  flag: `glob` when true, `substring` when false. We passed
  false.
- In 0.43 `expect_string_expression` builds
  `StringPattern::glob(value)` unconditionally. There is no
  opt-out, so the default moved to glob.
- A revset like `description(foo)` therefore went from
  matching any description containing "foo" to matching the
  literal "foo". Nothing of ours changes, since our revsets
  are `all()`, `children(<hex>)` and bare change ids, none of
  which take string patterns. A user-supplied
  `-r 'description(foo)'` does change.

We think this is worth recording because of what it says
about the mutation decision this cycle is deciding. Two
releases of a pre-1.0 library produced one break the compiler
caught and one it structurally could not, and the green build
that followed the fix was not evidence the bump preserved
behavior. That asymmetry is the treadmill cost, and it is
paid on every bump, not only the ones that touch the op
store.

**The clone test ran in a different network context than the failure.** Your shell reaches GitHub directly; my Bash tool goes through a sandbox proxy, which is what emitted `W CONNECT github.com:22: Bad Gateway` — that's socat, the proxy, refusing to open the SSH tunnel, not git failing to authenticate. Both of the forms you tried passed a clone URL where gh expects a username, and it rejected the string as a handle. Nothing there says anything about whether gh can reach the API; `gh auth status` or `gh api user` would be the actual connectivity checks.

content.text:
Confirmed, and the answer splits cleanly.

**For this failure, the gain is modest.** Our error was `Git process failed: External git program failed: fatal: Could not read from remote repository`. In jj-lib that arrives as:

```rust
GitPushError::Subprocess(GitSubprocessError::External(String))
```

`External(String)` is a string carrier. So we'd learn that the failure came from the external git process rather than `NoSuchRemote`, `UnsupportedGitOption`, `SpawnInPath`, or `Wait` — genuinely more than today, where every failure is one undifferentiated `Err(String)`. But the transient-versus-permanent distinction lives entirely inside that string, which is the same string we'd have to parse now.

The reason it stays a subprocess at all: jj pushes over SSH by invoking the external `git` binary, since gix has no SSH transport. Going in-process doesn't remove that subprocess — it wraps it in a typed error.

**The principle worth taking away:** errors that originate *inside* jj-lib become typed and matchable; errors that originate in processes jj-lib itself spawns stay stringly, just better boxed. That's exactly why bugs.md #1 is the good case and this one isn't — the index lock is jj-lib's own, so it should surface as a real variant rather than stderr text.

**And a caveat on "implied it was transient."** Typed errors almost never carry a retryable flag; jj's don't. You still hand-classify which variants you'll retry. What changes is that you match a *variant* instead of a *substring*, so your classification survives jj rewording its messages — which is the actual fragility, since that wording is UI text with no stability promise. Real improvement, but it's robustness of the matching, not the arrival of new information.

One practical note for the retry logic whenever it gets built: `SpawnInPath` and `UnsupportedGitOption` are clearly never retryable, `External` sometimes is, and treating the whole `Subprocess` arm as retryable would loop forever on a missing git binary.
